name: Seoul
info: Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, on the Han River in the north-west of the country. Baekje founded its capital in the area in 18 BCE, and Seoul became the capital of the Joseon dynasty in 1394.

facts.founded: Baekje founded its capital, Wiryeseong, in 18 BCE, believed to lie within the bounds of present-day Seoul; Yi Seong-gye, founder of the Joseon dynasty, chose Hanyang as his new capital in September 1394, and construction began in October 1394.
facts.where: On both banks of the Han River in the north-west of South Korea, in a mountainous and hilly landscape with Bukhansan on its northern edge.
facts.known: Wiryeseong, the capital of Baekje; the Joseon capital of Hanyang and Hanseong; the Fortress Wall and its gates; the Five Grand Palaces; Japanese rule as Keijo; the four battles for the city in the Korean War; the rebuilding of the city and the growth of Gangnam
facts.today: Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, with about 9.6 million residents, and the only special metropolitan city in the country.

t: Baekje founded its capital in the area in 18 BCE, Silla took the region in 553, and Goryeo built a southern capital there before the Joseon dynasty made Hanyang its planned capital in 1394.
Under Japanese rule from 1910 the city was renamed Gyeongseong and lost its status as a capital; it took the name Seoul after 1945, and four battles for it in the Korean War left it mostly in ruins.
After the war the city was rebuilt and in 1963 more than doubled in size, taking in Gangnam; its population peaked at over 10 million and has since decreased.
dyk: In the Korean War Seoul changed hands four times between June 1950 and the spring of 1951, and one estimate puts the damage at no fewer than 191,000 buildings, 55,000 houses and 1,000 factories in ruins.

sections.origins:
Seoul lies on the Han River in the north-west of South Korea. There is evidence of human habitation in the area from 30,000 to 40,000 years before the present. Around 4000 BCE people there lived in huts with lowered floors called umjip, and cooked grain and fish were being eaten by 3000 BCE. The Amsa-dong Prehistoric Site in Gangdong District, whose remains date to about 3,000 to 7,000 years ago, is the only known major Stone Age site in Seoul, since the city's heavy urbanisation has covered the rest.

When Wiman Joseon fell in the north (194 to 108 BCE), many refugees went south to the Han River basin, then controlled by Jin. They brought the culture and technology of the Chinese Warring States, which quickened the region's passage into the Iron Age. Jin disintegrated and dozens of small states competed for influence. Baekje, once one of the states of the Mahan confederacy, became the dominant local power by the 2nd century CE.

In 18 BCE Baekje founded its capital, Wiryeseong, which is believed to lie inside modern Seoul. Its exact location is not known with certainty. The earthen walls of Pungnap Toseong and Mongchon Toseong, in the south-east of the present city, date from the early Baekje period, and Pungnap Toseong is widely believed to be the main site of Wiryeseong. Both lie south of the river, away from the historic centre of Seoul in Jongno District.
sections.growth:
Seoul became a larger settlement only from the time of Goryeo, which built a summer palace there that was called the Southern Capital. King Sukjong built a palace near the site of the later Gyeongbokgung in 1104, and the city grew into a full-scale city with political significance in this period. It was thought that the kingdom controlling the Han River valley would also have strategic control of the whole peninsula, because the valley was a centre of transport.

The city's great expansion began in 1394, when it became the planned capital of the Joseon dynasty. Hanyang was designed as a geographic embodiment of Korean Confucianism, and the Fortress Wall that surrounded it was partly finished around 1396. In the late 19th century, after hundreds of years of isolation, the city opened its gates to foreigners and began to modernise. It became the first city in East Asia to have electricity, trolley cars, water, telephone and telegraph systems all at once, much of it through trade with France and the United States.

After the Korean War the city turned to reconstruction, and from the 1960s its economy grew rapidly. In 1963 two expansions more than doubled its area, from about 268 km2 to 613 km2. The second took in the area of present-day Gangnam, which was developed with the Hannam Bridge (1966 to 1969) and the Gyeongbu Expressway (1968 to 1970). The city's population peaked at over 10 million and has gradually decreased since 2014.
sections.rulers:
Baekje held the area as the site of its capital until Silla took control of the region in July or August 553. It became part of a newly established Sin Province and in 557 of Bukhansan Province. In 568 Silla's king Jinheung visited the area, set up a stele and made the city the capital of Namcheon Province. Goguryeo attacked Bukhansanseong in 603 and Silla won; in 604 Namcheon Province was abolished and Bukhansan Province re-established. Names used in this age included Bukhansan-gun under Goguryeo and Namcheon under Silla.

Goryeo, which succeeded Unified Silla, built its Southern Capital here. In 1392 Yi Seong-gye enthroned himself as king at the old Goryeo capital, renamed his kingdom Joseon in 1393 and in September 1394 chose Hanyang as the site of a new capital. The city, later called Hanseong, remained the Joseon capital until the fall of the dynasty. After Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 it was temporarily called Hwangseong, 'the imperial city'.

Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and renamed the city Gyeongseong (Keijo in Japanese). On 1 October 1910 it was reduced to a city like any other in Gyeonggi Province. In 1945 the American military took control, and the charter of 10 October 1946 gave the city the name Seoul. The new Republic of Korea adopted it as its capital. During the Korean War the capital was temporarily moved to Busan. In 2004 the Constitutional Court ruled that Seoul must remain the national capital as an 'unwritten constitutional custom', unless a nationwide referendum decided otherwise, although many ministries have since moved to Sejong City.
sections.life:
In the Joseon period the city was governed by the Hanseongbu, an agency of the national government. It divided the area into the part inside the Fortress Wall and the area of 10 ri around the wall, about 4 km out. The inner part, known informally as the area inside the Four Great Gates, was the city's only downtown. The wall was built to regulate visitors from other regions, to protect the city if it was invaded, and to guard against wild animals such as tigers and against thieves. Each day the gates were opened and closed to the ringing of large bells. Jongno, 'Bell Street', was one of the earliest commercial streets and is the site of the pavilion Bosingak with its large bell. The Namdaemun Market is the oldest continually running market in Seoul.

The population of the city was long almost entirely Korean. Foreign residents increased from the 1990s, among them English teachers and labourers from other Asian countries. The two major religions of present-day Seoul are Christianity and Buddhism, with Muism, the indigenous religion, and Confucianism also present. In the 2015 census 35 per cent followed Christianity, 10.8 per cent Buddhism and 53.6 per cent no religion. The city has the Seoul Central Mosque, opened in 1976, and the Yoido Full Gospel Church, which has around 830,000 members.

Bukchon and Namsangol Hanok Villages are old residential districts of traditional Korean houses. The stream Cheonggyecheon, which runs through the old city, was covered with concrete for many years and was restored in 2005.
sections.crises:
Silla and Baekje fought for the Han River region. In 554 Baekje and Gaya tried to retake it, and the Silla army under Kim Mu-ryeok defeated the combined force. Annexation by Japan in 1910 removed the city's standing as a capital and reduced its area. The Japanese authorities removed the city walls, paved roads and built Western-style buildings, and in 1936 annexed Yeongdeungpo as an industrial area for steel and other metalworking. The city was liberated by American forces at the end of the Second World War.

The Korean War did the greatest harm. Seoul fell to North Korean forces in the First Battle of Seoul in June 1950, was recaptured by United Nations forces in September 1950, fell to a combined Chinese and North Korean force in January 1951 and was retaken by United Nations forces in Operation Ripper in the spring of 1951. One estimate states that at least 191,000 buildings, 55,000 houses and 1,000 factories lay in ruins. A flood of refugees swelled the population, and estimates of its size differ, at 1.5 million for the city and its metropolitan area by 1955 or at 2.5 million, with more than half of them homeless.

Floods were a hurdle for the development of Gangnam, a low-lying area, and an expressway that doubled as an embankment was built there in 1967. A building collapse in 1995, caused mainly by rushed construction, killed over 500 people. On 29 October 2022 a crowd crush killed at least 156 people, among them at least 19 foreign nationals. Namdaemun, until an arson attack in 2008 the oldest wooden gate, reopened after complete restoration in 2013.
sections.legacy:
The Joseon dynasty built the Five Grand Palaces in Seoul: Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Gyeongbokgung and Gyeonghuigung. Changdeokgung was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997 as an outstanding example of Far Eastern palace architecture and garden design, and Gyeongbokgung has been restored on a large scale. The Fortress Wall of Seoul survives in part, and its gates include the south gate, Namdaemun, and the east gate, Dongdaemun. The Government-General Building of the Japanese period, which housed the colonial government, was torn down in 1995.

The name Seoul comes from the native Korean common noun seoul, 'capital city', believed to descend from Seorabeol, which referred to Gyeongju, the capital of Silla. The word was used colloquially for the capital as early as the 17th century, and French missionaries wrote the name Seoul, which is the origin of the romanisation in use. The Japanese authorities named the city Keijo, 'capital city', and after the liberation of Korea Seoul became the official name. In 2005 the city changed its official Chinese name from Hancheng to Shouer.

North Korea claimed Seoul as its de jure capital until 1972. Seoul is now the capital and largest city of South Korea and the only special metropolitan city in the country. It is divided into 25 districts, has about 9.6 million residents, and its metropolitan area contains more than half of the country's population. The planned city of Sejong, opened in 2012, has become the administrative seat of many ministries.

summary: Seoul, on the Han River in the north-west of South Korea, was the site of the Baekje capital Wiryeseong from 18 BCE and became the capital of the Joseon dynasty in 1394. It was renamed Gyeongseong under Japanese rule, was mostly ruined in the Korean War, and is now the capital of South Korea.
notes: START: both articles give 18 BCE for Baekje founding Wiryeseong, believed inside modern Seoul (exact site uncertain); I used -18, circa false.

DISAGREEMENT, Goryeo palace: the main article says Goryeo built a summer palace in the 11th century; the History article says King Sukjong built it in 1104 (12th century). In growth I attribute 1104 to 'one article' and left the century out; please check wording.

DISAGREEMENT, refugee population after the Korean War: the main article says an estimated 1.5 million by 1955 (city and metropolitan area), the History article 2.5 million, more than half homeless. I gave both with attribution; the editor may prefer to cut the figures.

DISAGREEMENT, Fortress Wall: the main article says about two thirds remains and six of eight gates; the History article says the wall no longer stands outside the northern mountains. I left out the fraction and named only the gates Namdaemun and Dongdaemun. The Joseon wall is also called a 20-foot stone fortress in the History article, not used.
DISAGREEMENT, Bronze Age: main article says about 1,500 BCE, History article about 700 BCE; left out.

DISAGREEMENT, Silla conquest: main article 'July or August 553'; History article gives a 554 battle (Kim Mu-ryeok defeating Baekje and Gaya). I give 553 for the take-over and 554 for the battle as the articles state them; they may describe the same conflict.

LEFT OUT, garbled passage: the main article's Silla section argues that Hanseong, Bukhansan and Pyongyang of the Three Kingdoms period referred to places near modern Pyongyang and that Namcheon/Bukhansan Province did not lie in Seoul. This conflicts with the same article's toponymy and with the History article; I used the provinces only as the article lists them under Silla (Sin, Bukhansan, Namcheon) and flagged them here as doubtful. Please read the rulers section first.
Joseon 1392/1393/1394: Yi Seong-gye enthroned 1392, renamed the kingdom 1393, chose Hanyang September 1394 (main article); History article says the capital was moved in 1394.
The main article's contemporary history says the charter was published 'on October 10 of the following year' after 1945, so 1946; used. 'Kyeongseongbu' name in 1945 left out.

Population: about 9.6 million 'as of 2024' written without the year; peak 'over 10 million', decreasing since 2014. 'More than half of South Korea's population' is said of the Seoul Metropolitan Area (Seoul, Gyeonggi, Incheon); the legacy paragraph says 'its metropolitan area'.
The 1936 annexation of Yeongdeungpo is given with a date in the main article; History says 1936 also. 1914 outer districts passed to Goyang County (History article), left out.
Names of the Joseon period: History article glosses Hanseong as 'Fortress city on the Han River'; main article calls Hanseong the Joseon-era name. Both used loosely.

Left out as outside the history brief: air quality, climate, economy, rankings, transport, sports, tourism, sister cities, Sejong's ministry count, the 2004 relocation plan to Gongju beyond the Constitutional Court ruling.
The Constitutional Court ruling is dated 2004 in the main article and 21 October 2004 in the History article.
